pos: n. (authority for an act; and, in Reformed pastoral theology, the ground on which a sinner may come to Christ)
etymology: Old French warant, a protector or authorisation. The warrant of faith was the great pastoral question of the seventeenth and eighteenth centuries: what entitles this sinner to believe?
biblical_def: The warrant of faith is what authorises a sinner to come to Christ, and Scripture makes it the command and offer of God rather than anything in the sinner. The invitation is unrestricted: “Ho, every one that thirsteth, come ye to the waters, and he that hath no money; come ye, buy, and eat” (Isa 55:1); “Come unto me, all ye that labour and are heavy laden, and I will give you rest” (Mat 11:28). The guarantee is absolute: “him that cometh to me I will in no wise cast out” (John 6:37). The last page repeats it: “whosoever will, let him take the water of life freely” (Rev 22:17). And the message itself carries the entitlement: “This is a faithful saying, and worthy of all acceptation, that Christ Jesus came into the world to save sinners; of whom I am chief” (1Ti 1:15).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines warrant as an act, instrument or obligation, by which a person is authorized to do something; that which authorizes; a commission; and a voucher, that which attests or proves.
webster_full: WARRANT, n. An act, instrument or obligation, by which a person is authorized to do something.
2. A commission which gives authority.
3. That which authorizes; that which vouches; attestation.
WARRANT, v.t. To authorize; to give authority or power to do or forbear any thing.
2. To maintain; to support by authority or proof.
scriptures: Isa 55:1
Ho, every one that thirsteth, come ye to the waters, and he that hath no money; come ye, buy, and eat; yea, come, buy wine and milk without money and without price.
Come unto me, all ye that labour and are heavy laden, and I will give you rest.
John 6:37
All that the Father giveth me shall come to me; and him that cometh to me I will in no wise cast out.
And the Spirit and the bride say, Come. And let him that heareth say, Come. And let him that is athirst come. And whosoever will, let him take the water of life freely.
This is a faithful saying, and worthy of all acceptation, that Christ Jesus came into the world to save sinners; of whom I am chief.
corruption_summary: A sinner is told to look inside himself for evidence that he may come, and the warrant is entirely outside him.
corruption_paragraphs: This was the great pastoral crisis of the hyper-Calvinist chapels, and the reasoning that produced it was not stupid. If Christ died for the elect, and a man does not know whether he is elect, on what authority does he come? The answer given in some quarters was that he must first find in himself a warrant — a sufficient conviction of sin, an inward drawing, a sense of interest in Christ — and only then venture. The effect was to bar anxious sinners from the Saviour until they could produce credentials, which is the exact reverse of the gospel.

The reply, argued by Andrew Fuller under the title The Gospel Worthy of All Acceptation, is that the warrant is the command and offer of God in the gospel, which is addressed to sinners as sinners. First Timothy 1:15 supplies the phrase: the saying is worthy of all acceptation — it deserves to be accepted by everyone who hears it, and the acceptance is therefore a duty rather than a presumption. John 6:37 removes the last hesitation with a double negative the AV keeps: him that cometh to me I will in no wise cast out. No qualification of the comer is stated anywhere in the sentence.

The practical form of the doctrine is what a pastor says to a frightened person, and it should be very simple. He is not to be sent away to examine his repentance, or to wait for a better frame, or to establish that he is among the elect — election is God's business and is known afterwards, by its fruits, not before, as a condition of coming. Isaiah 55:1 addresses the man who has no money, which is to say nothing to bring. That is the warrant, and it is the only one anyone has ever had.
roots_summary: Greek erchomai (G2064), to come; ekballo exo (G1544), to cast out; apodoche (G594), acceptation; Hebrew hoy (H1945), ho! — the summons of Isaiah 55:1.
roots_lines: Greek ou me ekbalo exo (G1544) — I will in no wise cast out; John 6:37 — a double negative of the strongest kind.
Greek pases apodoches axios (G594) — worthy of all acceptation; 1 Timothy 1:15, 4:9.
Greek ho thelon (G2309) — whosoever will; Revelation 22:17, and pas, every one, Isaiah 55:1 LXX.
usage: “He that hath no money; come ye, buy, and eat” — nothing to bring is the qualification.
“I will in no wise cast out” — and no qualification of the comer is stated.
“Worthy of all acceptation” — therefore accepting it is a duty.

pos: adj. (fixed; settled by decision beforehand — the AV's word for God's counsel at Acts 2:23)
etymology: Latin determinare, to bound or fix a limit, from terminus, a boundary. A determinate counsel is one whose bounds are already set.
biblical_def: Determinate means fixed beforehand. Peter uses it of the crucifixion: Christ was “delivered by the determinate counsel and foreknowledge of God”, and in the same sentence, “ye have taken, and by wicked hands have crucified and slain” (Act 2:23). The praying church repeats it: Herod, Pilate, the Gentiles and Israel gathered together “for to do whatsoever thy hand and thy counsel determined before to be done” (Act 4:28). It governs nations: God “hath determined the times before appointed, and the bounds of their habitation” (Act 17:26). The Lord says it of His own betrayal: “the Son of man goeth, as it was determined: but woe unto that man by whom he is betrayed!” (Luk 22:22). And Ephesians states the scope: God “worketh all things after the counsel of his own will” (Eph 1:11).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines determinate as limited; fixed; definite; and established, settled, positive, as a determinate rule or purpose.
webster_full: DETERMINATE, a. Limited; fixed; definite; as a determinate quantity of matter.
2. Established; settled; positive; as a determinate rule or order.
3. Decisive; conclusive; as a determinate judgment.
4. Resolved on.
5. Fixed; resolute.
scriptures: Act 2:23
Him, being delivered by the determinate counsel and foreknowledge of God, ye have taken, and by wicked hands have crucified and slain:
Act 4:28
For to do whatsoever thy hand and thy counsel determined before to be done.
And hath made of one blood all nations of men for to dwell on all the face of the earth, and hath determined the times before appointed, and the bounds of their habitation;
And truly the Son of man goeth, as it was determined: but woe unto that man by whom he is betrayed!
Eph 1:11
In whom also we have obtained an inheritance, being predestinated according to the purpose of him who worketh all things after the counsel of his own will:
corruption_summary: The decree is used to excuse the actor, and every text that states it states human guilt in the same breath.
corruption_paragraphs: The objection writes itself: if the crucifixion was determined beforehand, how were the men who did it guilty? Scripture never answers by weakening either half. Acts 2:23 puts both in one sentence — delivered by the determinate counsel and foreknowledge of God, and by wicked hands crucified and slain — and Peter says it to the very men who did it, as an accusation, and they are pricked in their heart. Luke 22:22 is even sharper because the Lord says both Himself: the Son of man goeth as it was determined, but woe unto that man by whom he is betrayed.

The Reformed have called this concurrence: God ordains the act, and the creature performs it freely and according to his own nature, and the creature's motive is his own. Joseph's brothers meant it for evil and God meant it unto good; both intentions are named in the same verse and neither is qualified. What the doctrine refuses is the idea that God's ordination supplies a man's motive. Judas was not made to want the money; he wanted it, and God's counsel did not fail on that account.

Acts 4:28 shows what the doctrine is actually for, since the church quotes it in a prayer under persecution. Threatened by the same council that had killed their Lord, they recite what Herod and Pilate had done and call it whatsoever thy hand and thy counsel determined before to be done — and then ask, not for escape, but for boldness. That is the pastoral function of a determinate decree. It does not answer the philosophical question; it tells a frightened congregation that the worst thing that ever happened was inside God's purpose, and therefore this is too.
roots_summary: Greek horizo (G3724), to mark out, determine; boule (G1012), counsel, purpose; proorizo (G4309), to determine before; prostasso (G4367), to appoint beforehand.
roots_lines: Greek horismene boule (G3724, G1012) — determinate counsel; Acts 2:23; the verb also Luke 22:22, Acts 17:26, 17:31.
Greek proorizo (G4309) — to determine before; Acts 4:28, Romans 8:29–30, Ephesians 1:5, 1:11.
Greek boule tou thelematos autou (G1012) — the counsel of his own will; Ephesians 1:11.
usage: “By the determinate counsel… ye have taken, and by wicked hands” — one sentence.
“As it was determined: but woe unto that man” — and the Lord said both.
“Whatsoever thy hand and thy counsel determined” — quoted in a prayer for boldness.

pos: n. (oversight; the care and direction of a superior — used of God's government of events and of His oversight of the writing of Scripture)
etymology: Latin super, over, and intendere, to stretch toward, attend to. The theological use is twofold: God's superintendence of history, and His superintendence of the men who wrote the Bible.
biblical_def: Superintendence is oversight from above. Over a man's plans: “A man's heart deviseth his way: but the LORD directeth his steps” (Pro 16:9). Over a ruler's decisions: “The king's heart is in the hand of the LORD, as the rivers of water: he turneth it whithersoever he will” (Pro 21:1). Over the writing of Scripture: “holy men of God spake as they were moved by the Holy Ghost” (2Pe 1:21), so that “All scripture is given by inspiration of God” (2Ti 3:16). And over a crime, without excusing it: “ye thought evil against me; but God meant it unto good, to bring to pass, as it is this day, to save much people alive” (Gen 50:20).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines superintendence as the act of superintending; care and oversight for the purpose of direction; and superintend as to have or exercise the charge and oversight of, to oversee with the power of direction.
webster_full: SUPERINTEND, v.t. To have or exercise the charge and oversight of; to oversee with the power of direction; to take care of with authority.
SUPERINTENDENCE, SUPERINTENDENCY, n. The act of superintending; care and oversight for the purpose of direction, and with authority to direct.
scriptures: Pro 16:9
A man's heart deviseth his way: but the LORD directeth his steps.
Pro 21:1
The king's heart is in the hand of the LORD, as the rivers of water: he turneth it whithersoever he will.
For the prophecy came not in old time by the will of man: but holy men of God spake as they were moved by the Holy Ghost.
All scripture is given by inspiration of God, and is profitable for doctrine, for reproof, for correction, for instruction in righteousness:
But as for you, ye thought evil against me; but God meant it unto good, to bring to pass, as it is this day, to save much people alive.
corruption_summary: Inspiration is imagined as dictation and providence as interference, and Scripture describes an oversight that leaves the creature entirely himself.
corruption_paragraphs: The two uses of the word illuminate each other. In 2 Peter 1:21 holy men spake — they did the speaking — as they were moved, borne along, by the Holy Ghost. Luke researched, David wept, Paul dictated in a temper, and the result in every case is the word of God. That is superintendence rather than dictation: the writer's mind, style, vocabulary and circumstances are all fully his own and fully governed, so that what he freely wrote is exactly what God said. The doctrine does not require a single verse to have been produced by a man in a trance.

Providence works the same way and Proverbs 16:9 states it in two clauses that neither cancel: a man's heart deviseth his way — the deliberating is real — but the LORD directeth his steps. Proverbs 21:1 applies it where it is least expected, to the most powerful and least accountable man in the society: the king's heart is in the hand of the LORD, and He turneth it whithersoever He will, as a farmer turns water down a channel. Neither verse suggests the king felt directed.

Genesis 50:20 is the doctrine at its hardest and most comforting, and Joseph says it to the men who did it: ye thought evil against me; but God meant it unto good. Two intentions, one act, and neither is a fiction. The brothers are not told their sin was really a favour, and Joseph does not pretend the pit and the slave train were pleasant; he says he will nourish them and their little ones, and speaks kindly to them. That is what a believer does with a superintended providence — not explain it away, but see far enough down the line to forgive.
roots_summary: Greek phero (G5342), to bear, carry along; theopneustos (G2315), God-breathed; Hebrew kun (H3559), to establish, direct; chashab (H2803), to devise, mean.
roots_lines: Greek hupo pneumatos hagiou pheromenoi (G5342) — moved, borne along by the Holy Ghost; 2 Peter 1:21; the same verb of a ship driven, Acts 27:15–17.
Greek theopneustos (G2315) — God-breathed; 2 Timothy 3:16 only.
Hebrew chashab (H2803) — to devise, mean, reckon; Genesis 50:20 — used of both parties in the verse.
usage: “Holy men of God spake as they were moved” — they spake, and were borne along.
“The king's heart is in the hand of the LORD” — and he did not feel directed.
“Ye thought evil… but God meant it unto good” — two intentions, one act.

pos: adj. (foreseeing and making provision; prudent in looking ahead)
etymology: Latin providere, to see beforehand, from pro-, before, and videre, to see — the same root as providence. God's providence is His seeing-ahead and providing; a provident man imitates it in miniature.
biblical_def: To be provident is to see ahead and provide. It is a Christian duty with a severe sanction: “if any provide not for his own, and specially for those of his own house, he hath denied the faith, and is worse than an infidel” (1Ti 5:8). It rests on God's own providing: Abraham named the mount “Jehovahjireh: as it is said to this day, In the mount of the LORD it shall be seen” (Gen 22:14). It is not anxiety: “Behold the fowls of the air: for they sow not, neither do they reap, nor gather into barns; yet your heavenly Father feedeth them” (Mat 6:26). Nature teaches it: the ant “provideth her meat in the summer” (Pro 6:8). And the promise stands: “my God shall supply all your need according to his riches in glory by Christ Jesus” (Php 4:19).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines provident as foreseeing wants and making provision to supply them; forecasting; cautious; prudent in preparing for future exigencies.
webster_full: PROVIDENT, a. Foreseeing wants and making provision to supply them; forecasting; cautious; prudent in preparing for future exigencies; as a provident man; a provident animal.
The parsimony of the miser is not to be confounded with the providence of the prudent.
PROVIDENTLY, adv. With prudent foresight; with wise precaution.
scriptures: But if any provide not for his own, and specially for those of his own house, he hath denied the faith, and is worse than an infidel.
And Abraham called the name of that place Jehovahjireh: as it is said to this day, In the mount of the LORD it shall be seen.
Mat 6:26
Behold the fowls of the air: for they sow not, neither do they reap, nor gather into barns; yet your heavenly Father feedeth them. Are ye not much better than they?
Pro 6:8
Provideth her meat in the summer, and gathereth her food in the harvest.
Php 4:19
But my God shall supply all your need according to his riches in glory by Christ Jesus.
corruption_summary: Trust and planning are treated as rivals, and Scripture commands both in the same breath.
corruption_paragraphs: The apparent tension is set up by reading Matthew 6 as a ban on planning. It is not; it is a ban on anxious thought, and the birds it cites are fed by a Father who nevertheless makes them fly out and find it. In the same Bible the ant is commended for gathering in summer, Joseph is honoured for storing grain through seven years, Proverbs praises the man who leaves an inheritance to his children's children, and Paul says a man who does not provide for his household has denied the faith. Improvidence is not faith. It is usually presumption, and sometimes it is laziness wearing a devotional vocabulary.

First Timothy 5:8 is the strongest sentence in the New Testament about family duty, and its severity is worth stating: worse than an infidel. An unbeliever with no doctrine at all generally feeds his own children; a professing Christian who does not has fallen below the standard of a man with no profession, and Paul says his profession is thereby denied. The context is the care of widows, which means the duty runs upward to parents as well as downward to children, and the passage assumes the family provides before the church does.

Genesis 22:14 supplies the theology that keeps providence from becoming self-reliance. Abraham names the place Jehovahjireh, the LORD will see to it, at the end of the hardest episode of his life, and the ram was in the thicket before he looked. The provident man plans and works, and knows that the provision he arranged for was itself provided; Philippians 4:19 promises supply according to God's riches rather than according to the planner's competence. Both halves are needed, and a man who has only the first is anxious and a man who has only the second is a burden to somebody.
roots_summary: Greek pronoeo (G4306), to provide, think of beforehand; Hebrew ra'ah (H7200), to see, provide; kun (H3559), to prepare; Greek trepho (G5142), to feed, nourish.
roots_lines: Greek pronoeo (G4306) — to provide for, take thought beforehand; 1 Timothy 5:8, Romans 12:17, 2 Corinthians 8:21.
Hebrew YHWH yireh (H3070) — the LORD will see, will provide; Genesis 22:8, 22:14.
Greek plerosei pasan chreian (G4137) — shall supply all your need; Philippians 4:19.
usage: “Worse than an infidel” — of a man who does not provide for his house.
“In the mount of the LORD it shall be seen” — and the ram was already there.
“Your heavenly Father feedeth them” — and they still fly out for it.

pos: adj. (not to be brought to agreement or friendship; implacable)
etymology: Latin in-, not, and reconciliare, to bring back into council or fellowship. The AV's word for the disposition is implacable and trucebreakers.
biblical_def: The irreconcilable man will not be brought to terms. Paul lists the disposition among the marks of a reprobate mind: “without natural affection, implacable, unmerciful” (Rom 1:31), and among the perils of the last days: “trucebreakers, false accusers, incontinent” (2Ti 3:3). Against it stands the Christian's obligation: “first be reconciled to thy brother, and then come and offer thy gift” (Mat 5:24) — the worshipper leaves the altar to do it. The rule is stated with its limits acknowledged: “If it be possible, as much as lieth in you, live peaceably with all men” (Rom 12:18). And the ground of all of it is the cross, “that he might reconcile both unto God in one body by the cross, having slain the enmity thereby” (Eph 2:16).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines irreconcilable as not to be reconciled; that cannot be appeased or brought to friendly terms; implacable; and, of things, incapable of being made to agree or be consistent.
webster_full: IRRECONCILABLE, a. Not to be reconciled; that cannot be appeased or brought to friendly accord; implacable; as an irreconcilable enemy or quarrel.
2. Not to be made consistent or congruous; as irreconcilable stories or statements.
IRRECONCILABLY, adv. In a manner that precludes reconciliation.
scriptures: Rom 1:31
Without understanding, covenantbreakers, without natural affection, implacable, unmerciful:
Without natural affection, trucebreakers, false accusers, incontinent, fierce, despisers of those that are good,
Mat 5:24
Leave there thy gift before the altar, and go thy way; first be reconciled to thy brother, and then come and offer thy gift.
If it be possible, as much as lieth in you, live peaceably with all men.
Eph 2:16
And that he might reconcile both unto God in one body by the cross, having slain the enmity thereby:
corruption_summary: Romans 12:18 is read as an escape clause, and it is a boundary on the other man's conduct rather than on one's own effort.
corruption_paragraphs: Romans 12:18 has two qualifications and they are almost always misapplied. If it be possible concedes that some reconciliations fail, because the other party may refuse and no one can be compelled into peace. As much as lieth in you is the demanding half: whatever portion of the matter is yours, all of it must be spent. The verse is not a permission to give up early. It is a statement that a Christian's responsibility ends at the boundary of his own conduct — and that within that boundary there is no residue left unspent.

Matthew 5:23–24 shows how far the obligation runs, and the direction of the offence is the surprising part. It is not if thou hast ought against thy brother but if thy brother hath ought against thee. The man with the grievance is elsewhere; the man at the altar is the one told to go. He leaves his gift, travels, and is reconciled first, and only then comes back to worship. A church full of unaddressed grievances is not offering acceptable worship, and the Lord puts the burden on whoever is aware of the problem rather than on whoever is at fault.

Ephesians 2:16 supplies the pattern and the power, and its verb is violent: reconciled both unto God in one body by the cross, having slain the enmity thereby. The enmity was not negotiated away; it was killed, and killed at cost. That is why a Christian's refusal to be reconciled with a brother is so serious a thing — it denies in practice what he claims to have received, and the parable of the unforgiving servant applies the arithmetic. Romans 1:31 puts implacable in a list of what human nature comes to when God gives it over, which means that implacability is not a personality but a symptom.
roots_summary: Greek aspondos (G786), implacable, admitting no truce; diallassomai (G1259), to be reconciled; katallasso (G2644), to reconcile; apokatallasso (G604), to reconcile fully.
roots_lines: Greek aspondos (G786) — implacable, refusing a truce; Romans 1:31, 2 Timothy 3:3 — both occurrences.
Greek diallagethi (G1259) — be reconciled; Matthew 5:24 only.
Greek apokatallasso (G604) — to reconcile completely; Ephesians 2:16, Colossians 1:20–22.
usage: “As much as lieth in you” — the demanding half of the verse.
“Thy brother hath ought against thee” — and thou leavest the gift.
“Having slain the enmity thereby” — it was killed, not negotiated.

pos: n. (the act of doing away with; the destruction or annulling of a thing)
etymology: Latin abolere, to destroy, do away. The New Testament's great abolition is of death itself, and the verb is used of Christ's work in three distinct places.
biblical_def: Abolition is a doing away. Its chief object in Scripture is death: our Saviour Jesus Christ “hath abolished death, and hath brought life and immortality to light through the gospel” (2Ti 1:10), and “the last enemy that shall be destroyed is death” (1Co 15:26). It is also of the wall between Jew and Gentile: Christ “abolished in his flesh the enmity, even the law of commandments contained in ordinances” (Eph 2:15). And of the fading glory of the old covenant: Moses put a veil over his face “that the children of Israel could not stedfastly look to the end of that which is abolished” (2Co 3:13), for “that which decayeth and waxeth old is ready to vanish away” (Heb 8:13).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines abolition as the act of abolishing; or the state of being abolished; an annulling; abrogation; utter destruction.
webster_full: ABOLITION, n. The act of abolishing; or the state of being abolished; an annulling; abrogation; utter destruction; as the abolition of laws, decrees, or ordinances, rites, customs, debts.
ABOLISH, v.t. To make void; to annul; to abrogate; applied chiefly and appropriately to laws, rites, customs.
2. To destroy, or put an end to; as, to abolish idols.
scriptures: But is now made manifest by the appearing of our Saviour Jesus Christ, who hath abolished death, and hath brought life and immortality to light through the gospel:
The last enemy that shall be destroyed is death.
Eph 2:15
Having abolished in his flesh the enmity, even the law of commandments contained in ordinances; for to make in himself of twain one new man, so making peace;
And not as Moses, which put a vail over his face, that the children of Israel could not stedfastly look to the end of that which is abolished:
Heb 8:13
In that he saith, A new covenant, he hath made the first old. Now that which decayeth and waxeth old is ready to vanish away.
corruption_summary: “Abolished death” is read as a denial that Christians die, and Christians go on dying while the verse stays true.
corruption_paragraphs: Second Timothy 1:10 says Christ hath abolished death — past tense, accomplished — and every believer since has died. The apparent contradiction is resolved by the Greek verb, which means to render inoperative, to put out of commission, rather than to make non-existent. Death remains as an event and has been stripped of its function: it no longer separates from God, no longer holds, and no longer terminates. Hebrews puts it as the destruction of him that had the power of death, and the deliverance of them who through fear of death were all their lifetime subject to bondage. The fact remains; the sting is gone.

First Corinthians 15:26 supplies the tense the first verse leaves out: the last enemy that shall be destroyed is death. So it is both done and not yet finished, which is the shape of nearly every New Testament blessing — the kingdom has come and is coming, we are saved and shall be saved, sin is defeated and must be mortified daily. A Christianity that keeps only the accomplished half becomes triumphalist and cannot handle a funeral; one that keeps only the future half has no comfort to bring to it.

Ephesians 2:15 shows the other great abolition and it is easy to miss how radical it was. The wall between Jew and Gentile was not a human prejudice to be overcome by goodwill; it was constituted by ordinances God Himself had given, and its removal required a death. Christ abolished it in his flesh, to make in Himself of twain one new man, so making peace. That is the ground of every reconciliation between hostile groups in the church, and it is not sentiment. It cost what it cost.
roots_summary: Greek katargeo (G2673), to render inoperative, abolish; kataluo (G2647), to destroy, throw down; aphanismos (G854), a vanishing away; aphtharsia (G861), incorruption, immortality.
roots_lines: Greek katargeo (G2673) — to render inoperative; 2 Timothy 1:10, 1 Corinthians 15:26, Ephesians 2:15, 2 Corinthians 3:13.
Greek aphtharsia (G861) — incorruption, immortality; 2 Timothy 1:10, 1 Corinthians 15:42–54, Romans 2:7.
Greek engus aphanismou (G854) — ready to vanish away; Hebrews 8:13 only.
usage: “Hath abolished death” — and believers go on dying.
“The last enemy that shall be destroyed” — done, and not yet finished.
“Abolished in his flesh the enmity” — and it cost what it cost.

pos: n. (meaning; the sense a sign conveys — the AV's word at 1 Corinthians 14:10)
etymology: Latin significare, to make a sign, from signum, a sign, and facere, to make. Every word is a sign; signification is what it is a sign of.
biblical_def: Signification is what a sign means. Paul's principle in the chapter on tongues is that meaning is the point of speech: “There are, it may be, so many kinds of voices in the world, and none of them is without signification” (1Co 14:10), and if the meaning is not known, “I shall be unto him that speaketh a barbarian” (1Co 14:11). John explains a saying of the Lord by its signification: “This he said, signifying what death he should die” (John 12:33). Agabus “signified by the Spirit that there should be great dearth throughout all the world” (Act 11:28). Revelation opens by the same verb: God “sent and signified it by his angel unto his servant John” (Rev 1:1).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines signification as the meaning of a word or sign; that which is intended to be expressed by a sign, word or symbol; and the act of making known by signs.
webster_full: SIGNIFICATION, n. The act of making known, or of communicating ideas to another by signs or by words, by any thing that is understood.
2. Meaning; that which is understood to be intended by a sign, character, word or expression; import; sense.
SIGNIFY, v.t. To make known something, either by signs or words; to express or communicate to another any idea, thought, wish, purpose or command.
scriptures: There are, it may be, so many kinds of voices in the world, and none of them is without signification.
Therefore if I know not the meaning of the voice, I shall be unto him that speaketh a barbarian, and he that speaketh shall be a barbarian unto me.
John 12:33
This he said, signifying what death he should die.
And there stood up one of them named Agabus, and signified by the spirit that there should be great dearth throughout all the world: which came to pass in the days of Claudius Caesar.
Rev 1:1
The Revelation of Jesus Christ, which God gave unto him, to shew unto his servants things which must shortly come to pass; and he sent and signified it by his angel unto his servant John:
corruption_summary: Religious speech is valued for its effect rather than its meaning, and Paul makes intelligibility the whole test of public worship.
corruption_paragraphs: First Corinthians 14 is the longest sustained argument in the Bible about language, and its conclusion is unfashionable: in the church, meaning outranks experience. Paul would rather speak five words with his understanding, that he might teach others, than ten thousand words in an unknown tongue. His analogies are drawn from music — a pipe or harp giving no distinction in the sounds, a trumpet giving an uncertain sound — and the point in each is the same: a noise that signifies nothing cannot do the work a signal does, however impressive it is.

Verse 11 contains the sharpest line: if I know not the meaning of the voice, I shall be unto him that speaketh a barbarian, and he that speaketh shall be a barbarian unto me. Both parties are foreigners to each other. That is the cost of unintelligible religion, and it is not confined to tongues. Preaching that runs on unexplained jargon, hymns whose words have never been unpacked, a liturgy recited by people who could not say what it asserts — each produces the same mutual foreignness inside a room full of people who think they are together.

The doctrine has a wider use, since the sacraments are signs and their signification is what makes them more than ceremony. Bread signifies a body given, water a washing, and a congregation that has forgotten what the sign is a sign of has kept the form and lost the speech. Revelation 1:1 is the Bible's own account of how symbolic language works: God signified it — gave it in signs — which is a warning against reading the book with no imagination and equally against reading it with nothing else.
roots_summary: Greek aphonos (G880), without voice, without signification; semaino (G4591), to signify, give a sign; semeion (G4592), a sign; dunamis tes phones (G1411), the meaning of the voice.
roots_lines: Greek ouden aphonon (G880) — none without signification, literally none voiceless; 1 Corinthians 14:10.
Greek semaino (G4591) — to signify; John 12:33, 18:32, 21:19, Acts 11:28, 25:27, Revelation 1:1.
Greek dunamis tes phones (G1411, G5456) — the meaning, force of the voice; 1 Corinthians 14:11.
usage: “None of them is without signification” — every voice means something.
“He that speaketh shall be a barbarian unto me” — and both parties are foreigners.
“Sent and signified it by his angel” — given in signs, on purpose.

pos: adj. (representing by figure or type; not literal, but conveying a real thing under an image)
etymology: Latin figura, a shape or form. The AV uses figure for the Greek tupos, a type, and antitupon, that which answers to it — the technical vocabulary of Reformed typology.
biblical_def: A figure represents a reality under an image. The tabernacle “was a figure for the time then present, in which were offered both gifts and sacrifices” (Heb 9:9). Abraham received Isaac from the dead “in a figure” (Heb 11:19). The flood prefigures a greater deliverance: “The like figure whereunto even baptism doth also now save us” (1Pe 3:21). Adam is “the figure of him that was to come” (Rom 5:14). And Paul reads Hagar and Sarah so: “which things are an allegory: for these are the two covenants” (Gal 4:24).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines figurative as representing something else; typical; representative; and, in rhetoric, changed from the literal sense, as figurative language.
webster_full: FIGURATIVE, a. Representing something else; typical; representative.
This, they will say, was figurative, and served by God's appointment but for a time.
2. In rhetoric, changed from the literal sense; as, a figurative expression.
3. Abounding with figures of speech; as a figurative style.
scriptures: Heb 9:9
Which was a figure for the time then present, in which were offered both gifts and sacrifices, that could not make him that did the service perfect, as pertaining to the conscience;
Accounting that God was able to raise him up, even from the dead; from whence also he received him in a figure.
The like figure whereunto even baptism doth also now save us (not the putting away of the filth of the flesh, but the answer of a good conscience toward God,) by the resurrection of Jesus Christ:
Rom 5:14
Nevertheless death reigned from Adam to Moses, even over them that had not sinned after the similitude of Adam's transgression, who is the figure of him that was to come.
Gal 4:24
Which things are an allegory: for these are the two covenants; the one from the mount Sinai, which gendereth to bondage, which is Agar.
corruption_summary: “Figurative” is used to mean unreal, and in Scripture a figure is a real thing that points to a greater real thing.
corruption_paragraphs: The word does most of its damage in arguments about the Lord's Supper, where this is figurative is heard as this is merely symbolic, and therefore nothing much is happening. That is not the biblical use. Hebrews 9:9 calls the tabernacle a figure, and the tabernacle was a real building where real blood was really shed; 1 Peter 3:21 calls the flood a figure of baptism, and eight souls really were saved by water. A figure in Scripture is a solid thing that carries the weight of a greater one, and calling something a figure raises its dignity rather than reducing it.

The Reformed have therefore held typology under strict rules, because the discipline is easily abused. A type is a divinely intended correspondence, and the marks of one are that the New Testament identifies it, or that the pattern is unmistakable and the theology fits — Adam and Christ, the passover lamb, the brasen serpent, Melchisedec, Jonah. What is forbidden is the allegorising that finds a secret Christ in every detail of every narrative, since a method that can prove anything establishes nothing and puts the interpreter's ingenuity in the place of the text.

Galatians 4:24 is the passage most often misused to license that, and it will not bear the weight. Paul says Hagar and Sarah are an allegory, and then reads them as the two covenants — but he is an apostle, he is arguing against people using the same narrative for the opposite conclusion, and the reading he gives is the plain theology of the two covenants rather than a hidden meaning. The safe rule for everyone else is that the literal sense governs, that figures are recognised by the text's own signals, and that nothing may be taught from a figure which is not taught plainly somewhere else.
roots_summary: Greek tupos (G5179), a type, figure, pattern; antitupon (G499), the answering figure; parabole (G3850), a parable, figure; allegoreo (G238), to speak allegorically.
roots_lines: Greek tupos (G5179) — type, figure; Romans 5:14, 1 Corinthians 10:6, 10:11, Acts 7:44.
Greek antitupon (G499) — the answering figure; 1 Peter 3:21, Hebrews 9:24 — both occurrences.
Greek parabole (G3850) — parable, figure; Hebrews 9:9, 11:19, and throughout the Gospels.
usage: “A figure for the time then present” — and the tabernacle was a real building.
“The like figure whereunto even baptism doth also now save us”.
“The figure of him that was to come” — said of Adam, by an apostle.

pos: n. (a false argument; reasoning that violates the rules of logic, especially one that deceives the reasoner himself)
etymology: Greek para, beside, and logos, reason — reasoning that has gone alongside the truth rather than at it. The verb paralogizomai occurs twice in the New Testament, and the second time it is a man deceiving himself.
biblical_def: A paralogism is reasoning that misses. The Greek verb appears exactly twice, and the pairing is the whole doctrine. Outward: “And this I say, lest any man should beguile you with enticing words” (Col 2:4). Inward: “But be ye doers of the word, and not hearers only, deceiving your own selves” (Jas 1:22). The same faculty that a deceiver uses on another, a man uses on himself. Isaiah names the terminal form: “Woe unto them that call evil good, and good evil; that put darkness for light, and light for darkness” (Isa 5:20). The remedy is examination: “Prove all things; hold fast that which is good” (1Th 5:21); and “rightly dividing the word of truth” (2Ti 2:15).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines paralogism as a false argument; a fallacy; or a fallacious argument, which the reasoner himself is deceived by.
webster_full: PARALOGISM, n. In logic, a fallacious argument or false reasoning; an error committed in demonstration.
PARALOGY, n. False reasoning.
FALLACY, n. Deceptive or false appearance; deceitfulness; deceit; that which misleads the eye or the mind.
scriptures: Col 2:4
And this I say, lest any man should beguile you with enticing words.
Jas 1:22
But be ye doers of the word, and not hearers only, deceiving your own selves.
Isa 5:20
Woe unto them that call evil good, and good evil; that put darkness for light, and light for darkness; that put bitter for sweet, and sweet for bitter!
Prove all things; hold fast that which is good.
Study to shew thyself approved unto God, a workman that needeth not to be ashamed, rightly dividing the word of truth.
corruption_summary: Bad reasoning is expected from opponents, and the New Testament's second use of the word is a Christian doing it to himself.
corruption_paragraphs: Webster's definition contains the distinction that matters and most dictionaries lose: a paralogism is a fallacy the reasoner himself is deceived by. A sophism is aimed at someone else; a paralogism has taken in the man who made it. That is why the Greek verb's two New Testament appearances belong together. In Colossians 2:4 a deceiver beguiles the church with plausible speech; in James 1:22 a hearer of the word who is not a doer is deceiving his own self by the same operation. The machinery is identical, and in the second case the victim cannot be warned by anyone he trusts more.

James goes on to describe the mechanism, and it is not intellectual: the man beholds his natural face in a glass, goeth his way, and straightway forgetteth what manner of man he was. The self-deception is achieved by not returning to look. A believer hears a sermon that names his sin exactly, agrees with it warmly, and by Tuesday could not say what it was about — and the agreement itself becomes the evidence that he is fine. Hearing has been substituted for doing, and the substitution is invisible from the inside because it feels like receptiveness.

Isaiah 5:20 shows where a long enough run of it ends: calling evil good and good evil, putting darkness for light. That is not a sudden inversion; it is arrived at by a sequence of small accommodations, each of which seemed reasonable when it was made. First Thessalonians 5:21 gives the only defence available — prove all things, test them, and the testing must include one's own conclusions. A man's reasoning about his own conduct is the least reliable he does, and it is the reasoning he examines least.
roots_summary: Greek paralogizomai (G3884), to deceive by false reasoning; pithanologia (G4086), persuasive speech; dokimazo (G1381), to test, prove; apatao (G538), to deceive.
roots_lines: Greek paralogizomai (G3884) — to reason falsely, delude; Colossians 2:4, James 1:22 — both occurrences, one outward and one inward.
Greek dokimazo (G1381) — to prove, test as metal; 1 Thessalonians 5:21, Romans 12:2, 1 Corinthians 11:28.
Greek apatao / apate (G538, G539) — to deceive, deceitfulness; James 1:26, Hebrews 3:13, Ephesians 4:22.
usage: “Lest any man should beguile you” — and the same verb, of oneself.
“Deceiving your own selves” — by not returning to the glass.
“Prove all things” — including one's own conclusions.

pos: n. (a guess; an opinion formed on evidence that does not amount to proof)
etymology: Latin conjicere, to throw together, from con- and jacere, to cast. A conjecture is a throwing-together of what is known in the hope of reaching what is not.
biblical_def: Conjecture is opinion beyond the evidence, and Scripture draws a boundary around it. The line is stated once for all: “The secret things belong unto the LORD our God: but those things which are revealed belong unto us and to our children for ever, that we may do all the words of this law” (Deu 29:29). The Lord forbids a particular conjecture: “It is not for you to know the times or the seasons, which the Father hath put in his own power” (Act 1:7). Judgment of persons is reserved: “judge nothing before the time, until the Lord come” (1Co 4:5). God's answer to Job is a series of questions: “Where wast thou when I laid the foundations of the earth?” (Job 38:4). And Paul ends his hardest argument in doxology: “how unsearchable are his judgments, and his ways past finding out!” (Rom 11:33).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines conjecture as an opinion or judgment formed on defective or presumptive evidence; a supposition; a guess; a surmise.
webster_full: CONJECTURE, n. Literally, a casting or throwing together of possible or probable events; or a casting together of circumstances.
Hence, an opinion or judgment formed on defective or presumptive evidence; probable inference; surmise; guess.
CONJECTURE, v.t. To guess; to judge by guess, or by the probability or the possibility of a fact, or by very slight evidence.
scriptures: The secret things belong unto the LORD our God: but those things which are revealed belong unto us and to our children for ever, that we may do all the words of this law.
Act 1:7
And he said unto them, It is not for you to know the times or the seasons, which the Father hath put in his own power.

Therefore judge nothing before the time, until the Lord come, who both will bring to light the hidden things of darkness, and will make manifest the counsels of the hearts: and then shall every man have praise of God.
Job 38:4
Where wast thou when I laid the foundations of the earth? declare, if thou hast understanding.
O the depth of the riches both of the wisdom and knowledge of God! how unsearchable are his judgments, and his ways past finding out!
corruption_summary: Conjecture is preached with the confidence of revelation, and Deuteronomy assigns the secret things elsewhere.
corruption_paragraphs: Deuteronomy 29:29 is the most useful verse in the Bible for a theologian and its structure is a division of property. The secret things belong unto the LORD our God; the revealed things belong unto us and to our children for ever — and the purpose clause governs both: that we may do all the words of this law. What is revealed is given for obedience rather than for speculation, and what is not revealed is not ours to reconstruct. A great deal of confident preaching about the unrevealed is trespass, and a great deal of comfortable ignorance about the revealed is theft.

Acts 1:7 is the Lord's reply to the last question the apostles ever asked Him, and it is a rebuke wrapped in a commission. They ask whether He will at this time restore the kingdom to Israel; He says it is not for you to know the times or the seasons — and then immediately, but ye shall receive power… and ye shall be witnesses unto me. The energy that would have gone into chronology is redirected into mission. Every generation's date-setting has ignored a verse spoken directly to the question, by the One who would know.

The other misuse is conjecture about people, and it is commoner in congregations than conjecture about prophecy. First Corinthians 4:5 forbids judging before the time until the Lord come, who… will make manifest the counsels of the hearts — and motives are precisely what no one can see. A church can and must judge conduct, which is visible; it cannot judge the heart behind it, and the confident attribution of motive is the most damaging conjecture ordinary Christians engage in. Romans 11:33 is where the honest theologian ends, and it is not a defeat: the doxology comes after eleven chapters of the hardest argument in Scripture, not instead of them.
roots_summary: Hebrew nistaroth (H5641), the secret things; niglath (H1540), the things revealed; Greek chronoi kai kairoi (G5550, G2540), times and seasons; anexereunetos (G419), unsearchable.
roots_lines: Hebrew hannistaroth / hanniglot (H5641, H1540) — the secret things / the revealed things; Deuteronomy 29:29.
Greek chronous e kairous (G5550, G2540) — times or seasons; Acts 1:7, 1 Thessalonians 5:1.
Greek anexereunetos / anexichniastos (G419, G421) — unsearchable, past finding out; Romans 11:33.
usage: “The secret things belong unto the LORD our God” — a division of property.
“It is not for you to know the times” — then, but ye shall be witnesses.
“The counsels of the hearts” — which is exactly what no one can see.
